EPDM Roofing for Winston-Salem Commercial Properties

EPDM has been on Winston-Salem's commercial roof stock longer than any other single-ply membrane, and a large share of what we get called out to inspect is an EPDM roof installed in the 1990s or early 2000s that's either due for recover or already past it. We still specify new EPDM where it's the right fit — it remains one of the more field-tested systems available, with a long track record on wide flat roofs.

Black vs. White EPDM

Traditional black EPDM has better flexibility in cold weather and slightly better puncture resistance in some formulations, which is relevant given the freeze-thaw cycling and occasional ice events Winston-Salem winters bring. White EPDM offers reflectivity closer to what TPO provides, at some tradeoff in seam-tape performance versus heat-welded systems. We spec color based on the building's cooling load profile and roof traffic, not by default.

Neither color changes the fundamental seam method: EPDM seams are taped or adhered rather than heat-welded, which means seam prep and adhesive cure conditions matter more here than on a TPO or PVC job, particularly in the humidity swings common through a Piedmont spring and fall.

Attachment Methods We Specify

Ballasted EPDM, held down with stone or paver ballast rather than mechanical fasteners, works well on structurally sound decks that can carry the additional dead load, and it's common on older industrial buildings around Winston-Salem where the original design already accounted for ballast weight. Fully adhered and mechanically fastened systems are the more common choice on buildings where added dead load isn't an option, or where a lighter-weight recover is the goal.

We calculate whether a deck can carry ballast load before recommending it, rather than treating ballast as the default low-cost option. A structural check is part of the proposal on any building where ballast is on the table.

  • Deck load calculation to confirm ballast is structurally viable, if proposed
  • Seam adhesive and tape system matched to ambient humidity and temperature at install
  • Attachment method selected between ballasted, fully adhered, or mechanically fastened
  • Flashing and penetration detail brought current to manufacturer standard
  • Existing membrane assessed for recover viability before new EPDM is proposed
  • Warranty tier confirmed against full assembly compliance

Recovering an Aging EPDM Roof

A large share of our EPDM work in this market is recover rather than new installation, on buildings around the older manufacturing and distribution stock near Winston-Salem and Kernersville where an EPDM roof installed decades ago is showing seam separation, shrinkage at the perimeter, or ponding that's outlasted the membrane's flexibility. Recover is viable when the deck and insulation test dry and the existing layer count is within what North Carolina's building code allows to remain in place; when it isn't, we specify tear-off instead.

EPDM on Institutional and Manufacturing Buildings

Some of the older buildings tied to Winston-Salem's manufacturing base, and some institutional roofs on campus-style properties, were originally built with EPDM and have a maintenance history that favors staying with the same membrane family for compatibility during future repairs. We'll recommend staying with EPDM in those cases rather than pushing a different system purely because it's newer to the market.

Compatibility When Recovering Over an Existing Membrane

Where an aging EPDM roof qualifies for recover rather than tear-off, we typically isolate the new membrane from the old surface with a cover board rather than adhering directly over it, since surface contamination, prior patch repairs, and uneven wear on the existing membrane can all interfere with new seam adhesive if the old surface is used as the substrate directly. The cover board also gives the new system a consistent, level surface regardless of what condition the original membrane is in underneath.

This adds a line item to the recover proposal that a lower-cost bid might skip, and we explain why it's there rather than leaving it as an unexplained cost. A recover that bonds new membrane directly to a compromised old surface is a common cause of early seam failure on buildings we're later called to inspect.

Warranty and Service Life Expectations

EPDM warranties follow the same material-only, system, or no-dollar-limit structure as other single-ply systems, tied to full assembly compliance and, in some cases, factory-certified installation. We document expected service life and warranty tier in the proposal so an owner is comparing EPDM against TPO or PVC options on equal terms, not guessing at long-term cost based on membrane type alone.

Frequently Raised Questions on EPDM Systems

Is EPDM still a good option compared to TPO?

It depends on the building. EPDM has a long field track record and can be the better fit where deck loading favors ballast or where an existing EPDM roof's maintenance history favors staying within the same membrane family.

How do you know if an EPDM roof can be recovered instead of replaced?

We core the membrane and check deck and insulation moisture along with existing layer count against code limits. If both test sound, recover is typically viable and gets documented in the proposal.

What's the difference between black and white EPDM?

White reflects more heat and reduces cooling load; black offers slightly different cold-weather flexibility in some formulations. We choose based on the building's cooling profile and traffic rather than by default.

Can EPDM be ballasted on any roof?

No. We calculate deck load capacity first, since ballast adds significant dead load that not every deck is designed to carry.

What warranty applies to a new EPDM installation?

Warranty tier depends on the manufacturer and whether the full assembly meets that manufacturer's current requirements; we confirm the tier in writing before the contract is signed.
